archetype.name: Super Bowl Contender (balanced)
archetype.definition: A team that ranks near the top of the league on both sides of the ball and has the point differential to prove it, so its 7-3 record undersells it more than it flatters it.

report.headline: Last year's luck became this year's efficiency; the Jaguars are the real thing.
report.take:
The 2025 Jaguars went 13-4, but that season ran on fumes: they led the league in wins over expected at 3.87 and covered more spreads than anyone. This year's 7-3 rests on firmer ground. Their net EPA of 0.222 ranks 2nd, the offense ranks 5th in EPA and the defense 3rd in EPA allowed, and their point differential per game ranks 1st. The point differential implies 6.2 wins against 7 actual, so this record is almost entirely earned. That is the difference between a team that got hot and a team that is good.

The defense is what drives it, and it wins in a specific way. It is the best run defense in football by EPA per play (-0.147, 1st), and opponents know it: they pass 4.3 points more often than normal against Jacksonville, the 4th-strongest pass funnel. Once they throw, the underneath game is shut off. EPA allowed on short passes ranks 1st and the tight end and lead back are the stingiest in the league as receivers. The weak spot is downfield and in the slot: deep EPA allowed ranks 21st and third receivers have found room. Trevor Lawrence has started every game and runs an efficient passing attack (7th in pass EPA), feeding Parker Washington far more than anyone else, while the line protects well enough and wins short yardage (2nd) even if it gets little push on early downs.

What the numbers flatter is the turnover margin. A league-best +1.1 per game, 17 takeaways against 9 giveaways, has turned several games into blowouts by handing the offense short fields. Some of that is a ball-hawking secondary playing with leads, but turnover margins this large rarely hold. What the numbers hide is how often this team beats itself with flags: 628 penalty yards, the line ranked 27th in penalties per game, and three games with 100 or more penalty yards, including the 23-18 loss to the Giants, where Lawrence also had his worst passing day of the year.

The path ahead is clear. The Jaguars hold a comfortable AFC South lead, play a 1-9 Titans team next, and then face a real test at 8-2 Chicago and against a Pittsburgh defense ranked 8th. A center injury (Robert Hainsey, a 91% snap starter, is out) is the most pressing on-field problem for an offense whose interior already ranks 30th in yards before contact.

strengths.title: A run defense that reshapes offenses
strengths.body: Jacksonville allows the fewest EPA per rush in the league, and opponents respond by abandoning the run more than almost anyone. That forces offenses into the short passing game, which the Jaguars also lead the league in stopping. It holds up because it comes from scheme and the front, not opponent quality: the run defense held a top-2 offense like Cincinnati to 23 rushing yards.

strengths.title: Efficiency on both sides, not luck
strengths.body: A net EPA ranked 2nd, a top-five offense and a top-three defense mean the record is backed by play-by-play quality. Unlike 2025, when the record outran the differential by nearly four wins, this team's differential supports almost every win. This kind of balance is the most durable profile in football.

strengths.title: Lawrence's efficient passing game
strengths.body: With Lawrence starting every week, the pass offense ranks 7th in EPA per play while protection holds up at a 10th-ranked sack rate. The offense has scored at least 31 in five of its wins, and it is at its best against weak secondaries, posting its best passing EPA days against Cleveland and Tennessee.

concerns.title: Self-inflicted penalties
concerns.body: The line ranks 27th in penalties per game and the offense has given away 628 yards to flags. It cost them in Cincinnati (won anyway), against Philadelphia (a two-point win as a big favorite) and in the Giants loss. This is a real flaw rather than a cost of aggression, and with a backup center stepping in it is more likely to get worse than better.

concerns.title: Turnover margin will cool
concerns.body: The league-best turnover margin has padded both the scoring offense and the points-allowed number by handing the offense short fields. The defense does force mistakes, but no team sustains +1.1 per game, and when takeaways dry up the margins in these games will narrow.

concerns.title: Pressure without sacks, leaks deep
concerns.body: The pass rush gets home often, with a pressure rate ranked 7th, but finishes poorly, with a sack rate ranked 30th. That gap, plus a deep-ball defense ranked 21st, is how good quarterbacks hurt this team, as Cincinnati's 428 passing yards showed. Against the stronger offenses left on the schedule, this is the matchup to watch.

trend.note: After a shootout loss to Houston, the Jaguars won three straight by 17 or more, then stumbled at the Giants with two turnovers, three sacks and 107 penalty yards. The underlying efficiency has been consistent all year, and the losses look like bad days rather than a decline.

nextGame.headline: A rematch with the Titans, two weeks after a 40-23 rout
nextGame.body:
Jacksonville beat Tennessee by 17 in Nashville in Week 10, throwing for 352 yards and its season-best passing EPA, and nothing about the Titans' profile suggests a different script at home. Tennessee's pass defense ranks 31st in EPA per play and dead last in explosive passes allowed. Its run-leaning offense (26th in pass rate over expected) runs straight into the league's best run defense. The Book has the Jaguars at -14.5 with a 47.5 total. The Titans' one real weapon is a pass rush that pressures at the 4th-highest rate.

Availability favors Jacksonville but not cleanly. Center Robert Hainsey is out, tackle Walker Little is questionable with a knee, and lead back Bhayshul Tuten is questionable after aggravating his ankle, though Liam Coen said the exam revealed nothing too bad. Tennessee has its own line issue, with tackle Dan Moore Jr. (96% of snaps) questionable on a line that already allows pressure at the 30th-ranked rate. Corner Cor'Dale Flott is questionable, and the Titans lost back Tyjae Spears to injured reserve, which thins a run game they lean on.

waysToWin.title: Throw at a broken secondary
waysToWin.body: Tennessee gives up the most explosive passes in the league and has been torched by opposing WR1s, which is Parker Washington's role here. Lawrence did exactly this in the first meeting. If Flott is limited, the Titans' coverage gets even thinner.

waysToWin.title: Take away the run, then the passer
waysToWin.body: The Titans want to run and are now without Spears; Jacksonville's run defense is the league's best by EPA. Forced into dropbacks behind a line that allows pressure at the 30th-ranked rate, possibly without Moore, Cam Ward faces a front that pressures at a top-10 rate.

waysToLose.title: The Titans' rush beats a patched line
waysToLose.body: With Hainsey out and Little questionable, Tennessee's 4th-ranked pressure rate is the one matchup where it holds an edge. If the interior breaks down, drives stall, sacks pile up as they did against the Giants, and Lawrence is pushed into hurried throws.

waysToLose.title: A Giants-style giveaway game
waysToLose.body: The last loss came as a 6-point favorite on two turnovers and over 100 penalty yards. An aggressive Titans team that goes for it on every fourth down can stay close if Jacksonville hands it extra possessions and short fields.

nextGame.watch: How Jacksonville's new center handles Tennessee's interior pressure on early downs. If Lawrence is clean, this goes the way of the Week 10 rout.

restOfSeason.body:
The efficiency profile is sustainable: elite run defense, a top-10 passing offense and a stable quarterback situation are not flukes, and the history shows this core produced a winning 2025 as well. Expect the turnover margin to drift toward ordinary, so the blowout scores and the 15-ish points allowed will likely creep up a little. The schedule also stiffens, with Chicago and Pittsburgh both bringing top-8 defenses and Dallas a top-3 offense.

The division should not be in doubt given the lead over Houston and a soft finish against Indianapolis. The real questions are seeding and whether the line's health and penalty habits hold up against good defenses. A bye-contending finish is realistic; a run of losses would most likely come from mistakes rather than being outplayed.
swingFactors: Center and tackle health on the offensive line
Games at Chicago and vs. Pittsburgh's defense

confidence.note: Ten games, one starting QB, and efficiency on both sides that matches the point differential.
